utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer I understand there is some technical problem which is thankfully limited to your case manager's machine. If the fellow wants to come in to fix it while we're in progress, he can do that, but I think we should get on with the case. You proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Bauer: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 80, good morning. Yesterday we stopped when you were describing how you got to know Mitar Vasiljevic before the war. When was the next time you saw Mitar Vasiljevic during the war, was that before or after the Uzice Corps left Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mitar Vasiljevic when the Uzice Corps had left Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe to the Court the circumstances under which you saw Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mitar Vasiljevic around the building and in the building in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing when you first saw him around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw him for the first time in front of the building where the garages were, and there were a couple of men with him, two or three, I don't know how many. Whether he was looking for people or wanted to break into the garages, I don't know. But anyway, I saw him near the garages the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe on what floor your apartment is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apartment is on the ground-floor level. It's really the first floor in the building. A higher ground-floor level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the windows are facing which side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The windows are facing the side where the garages were, and there was also another entrance to the building on that side. There were two entrances. One was from the street side and the other one was from the garage side of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far would you estimate are the garages away from your windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garages are roughly ten metres away. Well, sufficient distance for cars to be able to enter. About ten metres. I don't know for sure, but something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise anybody that came in to the garages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The incident when you saw Mitar Vasiljevic, what was he wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day; he was wearing some kind of black suit with a vest. He had a hat on his head. He looked like a cowboy, actually, in cowboy clothes. That's the impression that I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what colour the hat was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Light -- light brown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mitar Vasiljevic armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of arm did he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a rifle. I don't know much about guns, but I saw the rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, was it daytime or night-time you saw Mitar Vasiljevic that first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was daytime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a ribbon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did have a ribbon, a red coloured ribbon attached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long would you estimate did you look at this group of men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly. Briefly. He spent very little time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say -- was it ten seconds, one minute, five minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't dare look for long, but I could watch for five or ten minutes while he was around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually see him breaking into anything in one of the garages or did you just see him in front of the garages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I just saw him in front of the garages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which side would you say you saw Mitar Vasiljevic, from the front, the side, the back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him from the side, as my windows are facing the way the other entrance is facing. So I saw him from the side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any doubt in your mind that it was Mitar Vasiljevic whom you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any doubt, because I recognised him. So I never doubted for a moment that it was him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second time you saw Mitar Vasiljevic, was this shortly before you left town to Babin Potok?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did Mitar Vasiljevic look like that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, he had this hat on. He was dressed in the same way, the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mitar Vasiljevic do that day or what did you observe him doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, I saw him coming out of the entrance of the building I was in. He was leaving the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away was he approximately from your window when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entrance is about five or six metres from my windows. It's just the distance that is equal to the length of the corridor that leads to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look around in the courtroom, could you give us an approximate picture? Is it from where you sit up to the Judges' Bench approximately or further away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little further away perhaps. A metre or two further away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, at the time the witness was saying that, she was looking at the far wall. I'm wondering if she means a metre or two further than the far wall or from behind -- from the wall behind us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that for the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does this apply to me? Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The question was: The entrance from your window, was it about the distance from your seat where you're now seating to the Judges' bench or further away. You looked in another direction, actually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am looking in the direction where he is now, but to answer your question, a little further than the Judges are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer, my ability to estimate distances is befouled by a confusion between Imperial and metric to start with, but if somebody perhaps could later on measure the distance so that we have got at least some record or idea of the distance that the witness is referring to. And when she says to the Judges, I think she means to us rather than the bench or the wall. So it's where we're sitting. If somebody later on, if they could just measure the distance, we've got an idea then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: We will do so. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any particular thing about Mitar Vasiljevic you realised that day? About his way of walking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second time I saw him, he walked in a different way. One leg was being dragged. I couldn't look for long, but somehow he didn't seem to walk normally. It was one leg. I can't remember which one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any cast on his leg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see whether there was a cast or something else. I just noticed that one leg was sort of being dragged, that his steps were not normal, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VG80, did there come a time when an OTP investigator showed you an array of pictures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the accused in one of those pictures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Could the usher please --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Sorry. It is premarked Exhibit 20.VG80. Please don't put it on the ELMO, just to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the photo array you were shown?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign with your name and date it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's only one signature on the document, but I would be interested to know whether she saw it originally in colour or in black and white.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see it in a colour copy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw a black and white copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And was the one that she signed a black and white copy?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you answer His Honour's question, please? Was this the copy you signed or did you sign a black and white copy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a black and white or a colour copy, but I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got the original, Ms. Bauer?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think the confusion started -- the original was actually the colour copy. You have the colour copies in your binders, as does the Defence. Since we didn't have enough colour copies, we tendered the original colour copy as a piece of evidence and just gave for Your Honours for reference black and white copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're grateful for that, but I think we should have it clear each time this arises. That is very real difference between a photo identification from colour photographs and from black and white. Indeed in some cases I've been involved in, that was absolutely vital. I'm not suggesting it was in this case, but it is important to keep them separate. So the document which the witness has, has she got the one that she actually signed?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes. She has the one that she originally sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you just tell us we're being given black and white copies, it will save us having to ask this every time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right. Is there any objection to the tender of that document into evidence, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've lost the number on the screen now. What was it, 80? 8-0, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It was Exhibit 20.VG80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P20.VG80, and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VG80, would you be able to recognise the accused today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in court today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe where he is sitting and what he's wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's sitting to my left. He has a brown jacket, a white shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you say to the left, do you mean the first row to the left, the second row to the left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's only one person with a brown coat. I think we're safe. She is pointing to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet. Cross-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, do you remember sometime in 1994 having given a statement to the centre of the security services of the MUP in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 I gave the statement to the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That may be the one. Did you make that statement once?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, yes, once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that statement and what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember, and I will always remember what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement, madam, which is quite a lengthy one, consisting of some 17 pages, you described many events and many persons that you saw at the time, both Serbs and Muslims; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs, yes, but I could only rarely see Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I meant was that you mentioned them as victims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslims as victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement, you mentioned quite a number of Serbs who, according to you, were involved in various incidents and were members of paramilitary units in the area of Visegrad; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement, you mentioned many names, and for some very specific particulars.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I gave the particulars for all those that got hold of me and who personally mistreated me, and I gave the particulars regarding what I personally experienced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite so. You mentioned a large number of names of Serbs who participated in various paramilitary formations; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember and is it true to say that in that statement that you gave to the MUP, not once did you mention Mitar Vasiljevic, the person who is in court here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention Mitar Vasiljevic because at the time, I was under the effect of the other things. I was sick, and after everything I'd gone through, I had to say everything. Just then, I was not capable of listing them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you for that. I would just like us to establish, since in that report you mentioned more than 20 persons of Serb ethnicity, accusing them of very grave crimes, and it is quite possible that this sighting that you testified about today was not so important for you, for you to mention it. But you would agree with me that at the time, you did not mention Mitar Vasiljevic in any way whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my first statement, I didn't mention Mitar Vasiljevic, and I am repeating, because I was in a very bad state after everything. The fact that I saw him, he didn't personally do anything to me so that at first I didn't mention it, but I did later see him and I claim that I did see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. My question was only limited to this particular point. You mentioned him in the statement you gave to the investigator roughly in the same way that you told us today; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made that statement a few months ago, that is, in the course of this year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember or could you explain to me how it came about for you to testify about this or, rather, for you to be called to testify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I recognised him on the photograph because I saw him in Visegrad, and I wanted to say this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. What photograph did you recognise him on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph that I was shown a moment ago when I was looking for the Lukics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, this photo array on which you recognised Mitar Vasiljevic was shown to you when you were being interviewed by the investigator; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I will continue to look for all those who did what they did, on photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but that was when you were making your statement to the investigators. So my question was: How did it come about for you to report as a witness to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How it came about for me to report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say, and I personally will always demand to say. I don't know whether that's enough. Have I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is whether someone asked you to testify or did you yourself apply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I applied myself, and I will always apply. Nobody needs to ask me to testify. I personally will always volunteer to testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that you were looking at those photographs when you were identifying Lukic, I think you've said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is when I recognised Vasiljevic, and I asked him -- I asked that he, too, as an accomplice of all the evils.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told the investigator what you told us today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise Lukic as well and make a statement about him too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised Sredoje Lukic, and I always will recognise him, but Milan Lukic I saw in Visegrad for the first time, but I'm not sure I will recognise him, but I will do my best to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the time, as far as I could understand, you said you could not remember the date when these events occurred, is that right, but they were after the Uzice Corps left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the Uzice Corps left. I can't remember the date because I was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one question. Re-examined by Ms. Bauer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VG80, at the time you gave your first statement to the MUP, were you specifically asked about Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked about anybody else specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first statement was simply because I wanted to recount everything that happened to me. So they didn't insist on anyone. It was me who said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer, it may be only curiosity, but I would like to know which one on this that that is Exhibit 20.VG80 that she identified as Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VG80, when you were shown the photo spread you just were shown a minute ago, did you at that time identify Sredoje Lukic on that photo spread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG80 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Could, please, the exhibit be given to her again. She can have my copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us which number Sredoje Lukic is? Do you see him anywhere on this photo spread, VG80?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know how many photo spreads she saw --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: She probably saw another one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: To me, and I hope that Mr. Domazet will understand that it's only a matter of first impression, but the clearest indication that this evidence has given to me was that she was being asked to make a statement or assist in relation to one of the Lukics, that she probably had put on a statement with MUP, and it was in the course of being shown photo spreads that she identified the accused here. It perhaps does not matter very much, but it seems to me a first step towards confirming that if we know whether he, Sredoje Lukic, is on this particular photo spread.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't seen Sredoje Lukic yet, but basically I don't think he is on that photo spread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, Perhaps it's an unfair question. The other matter that I wanted to raise, it doesn't strictly arise out of cross-examination, but I do not think we have any evidence in the case as to the significance, if any, of the red ribbon to which reference has been made.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It is I mean, it is …the accused refers to a red ribbon. He explains it, I think, in a different form than the witnesses. So she ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I think he explains it having another purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid we weren't ….

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: But I think it was in the statement of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We weren't taken right through the statement, and I frankly, read only where we were taken, with a few pages perhaps on each end. So we'll find that in the statement, will we?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Would it assist if we point you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. I thought that if it was something of other significance this witness may be able to help, that's all. Now, is that all you wanted to ask her?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you VG80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, for coming here to give evidence. We're very grateful to you for the evidence you gave and you are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The next witness is Ms. Tabeau or VG61?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the after yesterday's session, Mr. Domazet informed me that he would be ready to resume the cross-examination of VG77. That witness is inside the waiting room, if you care to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go back to VG77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you understand that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you made yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet. Further cross-examination by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, yesterday you said and told us for the first time that you had seen Mitar Vasiljevic immediately prior to your departure from Visegrad on June 17th or 18th, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he mistreated you and tried to take you to the police station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what he was wearing on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. He was wearing military clothes. It was actually a masked -- camouflage uniform, and that is -- when I saw him, well, I just lost control of myself. I no longer paid attention to him. I looked at him only because he was threatening with a bomb, and he was waving his hand with it, and he was telling us to sit down, to get up, to sit down. We were all lost, because at that moment, we all expected to be dead. I didn't pay attention to anyone then because I simply did not know what was happening. Then he made us go to the SUP, to the police. I don't know who the person was. When we got to the police station, I wasn't aware of who he was. And then when someone said, "Mitar, where are you taking these people?" He said, "Kill them all. Kill them and nothing less" "Let them go," said something, "They have a convoy at 8.00 to go further on to Olovo." He said, "Kill them," and nothing else. I wasn't aware of who he was even then. I said that in this statement, but I was never aware of the fact that this was Mitar. It was only later when I gave thought to the matter following my statement. Then I recalled that the three persons when, they went down the stairs, when they said, "Mitar, let them go to their convoy."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you well, on the basis of the fact that someone called the person Mitar in front of the police station, you thought that the person was, in fact, Mitar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until then, you hadn't understood that it was him or recognised him. You recognised him on the basis of the fact that a policeman said, "Don't, Mitar"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because a woman told me, whose husband was in Glavica, to the left of Pionirska Street, he --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer our questions, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I asked you whether on the basis of a policeman saying, "Mitar, don't do this," that you understood that it was Mitar Vasiljevic in question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know or hear that there was a person who had been -- who was a member of a paramilitary formation and his name was Mitar Knezevic and his nickname was Mitar Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the experience I've had and the experience with my group, all of them have said, and they might come and confirm this, that the person in question was Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Domazet. May I remind both of you, please pause. Mr. Domazet, please pause before asking the question. And madam, would you please pause before answering the question to enable the interpreters to catch up. You are almost speaking on top of each other and it is very difficult for them. So just that pause. Not very long, but just enough. Say, count to five or six. That should be sufficient. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, can you remember or identify any person who was present from the police when that person that they referred to as Mitar came in front of the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know that they were policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, do you know any other Mitar? Did you know any other Mitar in Visegrad or in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because they talked about Mitar Vasiljevic only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask you, have you heard about any other Mitar, Mitar Chetnik, Mitar Knezevic as a member of one of the paramilitary formations? Have you heard of that name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your answer today, you will correct me if I'm wrong, that in an earlier statement to the investigator, this incident, although you consider it to be very serious indeed, you failed to mention because at the time you were not sure whether it was this Mitar in question, but it was only subsequently, when you remembered that the policeman referred to him as Mitar, you realised that it might have been Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome. Re-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 77, I want to ask you a couple of questions regarding this incident on the day you left Visegrad as well. The question I want to ask you is: The person you saw and described to this Court as being Mitar Vasiljevic that day, were you able to see this person's face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that particular moment, I saw absolutely nothing. I was lost. Not only me, but whole group felt lost, because at that moment, I was really shaken, and I felt as if I were flying, that I had wings, that I didn't have arms or legs. You didn't think about anything. You expected at any moment to be hit by something. Every second you expected that to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question in another way. Mr. Domazet asked you whether you recognised or whether this person could have been a person by the name of Mitar Knezevic. Mr. Knezevic is missing one eye. Would you have been able to see whether the person you've described as Mitar Vasiljevic was missing an eye on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I can't remember. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was going to ask you, Mr. Groome, there is going to be some evidence about that, is there? Because Mr. Knezevic is mentioned elsewhere. But there is some evidence going to be given that he has only one eye?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Defence has stated that they will present that evidence on their case, that that is the nature of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, all right. I'm sorry you have not finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is a matter arising from two answers that she gave in cross-examination that I will draw to your attention in a few moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps if you draw it to my attention now, Your Honour, I'm moving to a different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, when the witness was first recounting how she remembered or came to the conclusion it was the accused who was involved in this particular incident, at page 16, she said, according to the transcript: "I said that in this statement, that I was never aware of the fact that this was Mitar. It was only later when I gave thought to the matter following my statement. Then I recalled that the three persons, when they went down the stairs, they said, 'Mitar, let them go to their convoy.'" Now, that's the statement she said of her own volition, but then in the course of the cross-examination, at the very end of it, it's rendered a little ambiguous. I'm referring now to page 18: "From what you answered today, you'll correct me if I'm wrong, that in an earlier statement to the investigator this incident, although you consider it to be very serious indeed, you failed to mention because at the time you were not sure whether it was this Mitar in question. It was only subsequently, when you remember the policeman referred to him as Mitar, that you realised that it might have been Mitar Vasiljevic." Now, you see the difference there? In one place she's saying she put it in the statement, in another one she's saying she did not. That should be easily cleared up I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll do that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 77, you've had an opportunity to look at your statement that was taken earlier this year, in January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement, for whatever reason, you did not mention Mitar Vasiljevic -- as having seen Mitar Vasiljevic on the day you left Visegrad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It came to my mind later on, when I had thought about it. When I gave the matter further thought, when I was thinking about who it was and how the events evolved, and that moment I remembered when I heard someone say, "Mitar, let the people go," and then I realised that it was Mitar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first time an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor sat down and asked you these specific questions was approximately eight and one-half years after the events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that all you're going to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's still anything but clear to me as to whether the incident was referred to in the statement. It's simply that she didn't name Mr. Vasiljevic. That's the whole point of this. Because it's one thing if she put the incident in and didn't identify the accused as being responsible, and it's quite a different one if she didn't even put the incident in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 77, at the time you gave your statement in January of this year, did you describe the incident which you've described in court that occurred on the day you left Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now take you back to the portion of your cross-examination where Mr. Domazet was asking you about the home of a witness, 115, 115, and you were shown a piece of paper to tell you that name. Do you recall your testimony regarding this matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hundred and fifteen. Well, I cannot remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hundred and fifteen. A woman. A female person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the witness be shown that piece of paper that she was shown yesterday that indicated who number 115 was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, it was my copy of the list. I'll just see if I can find it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who we are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to that house. I was there on a number of occasions [redacted], but I never looked through the window to see whether the house could be seen, but I presume it could not have been seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now take you to the time in your testimony when Mr. Domazet was asking you about whether you saw the accused Mitar Vasiljevic on the television, and I want to ask you the following question: At the time that you saw the person you've identified as Mitar Vasiljevic on the television, did you immediately recognise him as Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw him briefly. I accidentally tuned in. I saw him very briefly, and I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise him before a narrator or some other information from the television identified him as being Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the person on the television as Mitar Vasiljevic before you heard any narrator or any newscaster identify this person as Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment I switched on the TV, it showed the courtroom. It may have been on television before, but I hadn't switched on the television before I saw all of this, and all of a sudden, I saw him, and then I said, "Ah, there is Mitar Vasiljevic under arrest."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question another way. Did you recognise him as Mitar Vasiljevic because of your own memory or because of something that was said on the television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG77 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised him, and at that moment, when I saw him when it was shown on television, I recognised him to be Mitar Vasiljevic, who was under arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming here to give evidence, madam, and for the evidence you gave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I? After this latest answer by the witness who claims that in her statement to the investigator she did speak about this incident that occurred just before she left Visegrad, may I ask for the Prosecutor's consent or, rather, admission that she made no mention at all of that incident in that statement, to avoid tendering that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just have a second to refresh my memory on the last paragraph. She refers to some incident that clearly doesn't mention the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's not the point, as I keep trying to make. Did she refer to the incident she described?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's why I'm trying to just look at this last and see ... Yes, Your Honour. I will agree that although she does mention being in the square at the time and place she's testified here, she does not mention being brought to the police station or being harassed in the way that she described here in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, the question you asked her in re-examination was this: "At the time you gave your statement in January of this year, did you describe the incident which you've described in court that occurred on the day you left Visegrad?" Now, your reference to the incident at the police station is sufficient to cover the whole of that, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. That will be noted that she did not in fact refer to this incident in her statement January of this year. All right. Now, who are we going to take next?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer is going to bring on Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hope that her evidence will be brief and that the statement that she has prepared, or report, will go into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, that was the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration on the document which the court usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bauer. Examined by Ms. Bauer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, just to establish your professional background --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to establish your professional background, have you been a graduate in economics and statistics and have a Ph.D. in mathematical demography from the University of Warsaw?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All of this is set out in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It is all set out in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just ask her to confirm whether the statement Summary of Professional Qualifications on page -- the first page, which isn't numbered, are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The summary of your professional qualifications that you set out in your report, are they correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is all correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then let me ask you; the task you were asked to undertake is to make a demographic study about the changes in the ethnic composition in the municipality of Visegrad between 1991 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what we were asked for.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Do we -- could I ask that the report at this time is already tendered into evidence? It is premarked P41.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Wait a minute. The document that I'm being handed is not the document we're talking of. What you are tendering is the 17th of August, 2001. Is that the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It is. It is the research report prepared for the case against Milan Lukic et al., and it is numbered P41.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The document which was filed was not marked that and I want the document which was filed. That will be Exhibit P41.1. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please briefly describe the methods you used in order to conduct your assessment.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This report takes the macro perspective, which means the perspective of the whole population who lived in the area of the Visegrad municipality in the period that we are interested in. The period that we were interested in was, of course, first of all, the year 1992, but because the necessary information, statistical information for this period is unavailable to us, we had to use other information, sources, and coming from other periods which, however, are highly relevant to the studying the changes in the ethnic composition in the Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We studied the ethnic composition in 1991, which is the latest year before the period of interest, 1992, and compared the ethnic composition in the Visegrad municipality in 1997, which was the year for -- the first year after the war ended for which we had some statistical, good statistical information. We --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 1991, could you just briefly explain which source that was you based your assessment on, and the same for 1992 -- for 1997.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For 1991 we used the population census which was conducted in Bosnia and Herzegovina and other republics of the former Yugoslavia. It was the last census and -- well, information -- last available information source that could be used in this report. For 1997, we unfortunately didn't have sources like that census, like the population census. Instead, we used the voters' register from the municipal elections in this year. The also elections took place in all the countries, Visegrad was just one of the municipalities for which we have information about the voters. So these were the two sources that we used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The reference to using the voters' register in the municipality this year, I'm not sure whether that means 2001 or 1997.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: 1997, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who assembled this voters' register?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The voters' register was established by the OSCE, Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, who actually was responsible or whose mandate included securing that the elections, post-war elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina were conducted in the proper way and optimal way. So they established the voters' register actually. First time not in 1997, but already in 1996. And in 1997, these voters that we used was actually an improved version of the register that was made first time for the 1996 elections. Shall I continue with the method?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that we've got it all in writing, all we want is a very brief summary --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Of the major findings. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think if you'd go to the findings. And if there is any questions about the methodology, no doubt, counsel if they want to know about them will ask you, but we've got a very, very detailed report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could we please move to the major findings. What was -- there was one other source I was missing that you mentioned. Could you please shortly say the third source you were using before we come to the major findings?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We also used the list of missing persons that was completed by ICRC. The list that we used for the analysis in this report was the 4th edition, which means an updated version of the list that actually started to be completed directly after the war or in some cases even during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that by linking the information between the 1997 voters' register and the 1991 census, you could confirm that about 82.5 per cent of the some 620 individuals missing, you could confirm the identity of these people?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. By comparing the persons, all actual details such as, for instance, names, date of birth, place of birth on the two lists, ICRC missing list on one hand and the population census on the other hand, we could make sure that the persons on the list of missing persons are real individuals who lived in 1991 and were enumerated, that means included in the population census. Actually, if I may add one thing. The individual linking approach was not only used in the analysis of the ICRC list of missing persons but all other analyses presented in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to the major findings. What did you -- what was the conclusion about the changes in the ethnic composition pre-war and post-war in the municipality of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: If I may refer to figure 1A.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Could we for this purpose please distribute to the Judges another document which would be pre-numbered Exhibit 41.2. And maybe for the public, could one copy or so be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So next page, please. I am referring to figure 1A, which is on page 2, next to front page, to the front page, and table 3A of this presentation is part of our report, and in our report, I included it under the same numbers. Figure 1A is a bar chart which shows four groups of bars. Each group is made for one ethnic group. The first two bars, which I call group 1 are shown for Serbs, the next one for Muslims, the next one for Croats, and the last one for others. In this figure, we compare the ethnic composition based on the information obtained from the 1991 population census, with the ethnic composition based on the information coming from the 1997 voters' register. In figure 1A, percentages are shown in table 3A, both things, absolute numbers, which means size, absolute size of each ethnic group in each of these years and also percentages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Let me summarise the picture in figure 1A. In 1991, the light coloured bars is the year 1991, actually, the majority group are Muslims, if you see it, from the table you can read that the Muslims constituted 62.5 per cent of the Visegrad population in 1991. Serbs 32.5 per cent. So these Serbs were the second largest group in the municipality of Visegrad in 1997. The picture is completely different. We observed that Muslims are not the majority group any more. Actually, there are no Muslims at all shown for 1997. Serbs, on the other hand, are almost the only group shown here in this figure. It is 95.9 per cent of the population of the Visegrad municipality who are Serb. So the conclusion is that the ethnic composition changed dramatically from 1991 to 1997, and apparently, in 1997, the municipality which used to be Muslim became actually Serb. This is the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next -- the next --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- page. You were examining the internally displaced population from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please describe your conclusions based on those two tables?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Now to illustrate our second conclusion, please look at figure 1B and table 3B. This is next page in the distributed materials. Again, both presentations are included in our report. This analysis, actually, it is slightly differently designed, constructed compared with the previous one. In this analysis, we took the perspective of all those who originally lived in the municipality of Visegrad in 1991, and we were able to find them in our information source, voters' register, 1997 voters' register. So it is the perspective, as we call it, of the municipality of origin, and we are trying in this analysis to show what is the -- what was the actual place of residence. We can call it this way, of those who were originally in the Visegrad municipality but in the year 1997. And we look not only at the internally displaced persons but also at the persons who migrated, which means left the country and moved to other countries. There is this big difference between those two terms, displaced person and a person who migrated, a migrant. These displaced persons are almost always internally moved to other places. If you please look at the table, you see that we show that voters -- 1997 voters, by ethnicity of course, using three categories. One category is, this municipality means the Visegrad municipality. Here in this column, those voters are shown who didn't move elsewhere but stayed in the Visegrad municipality in 1997, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is not quite clear to me, when you look at the absolute numbers, this deals only with 4.535 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Where there 11.238 in the earlier map?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, previous presentation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now does this mean that it's only -- that you could find the whereabouts of 4.535 Muslims or is that -- even when you add the 2.000 -- I'm sorry, the total is 6.602. What has happened to the 5.000-odd that were living within the Visegrad municipality in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, this is, first of all, the year 1997. So as you very correctly remarked, the number of Muslims in the Visegrad municipality was much higher in 1991 as presented in the table 3A. It is correct that we were unable to identify all Muslims that were included, listed in the population census in the voters' register for 1997. We were unable to find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you, madam, I just wanted to know?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They could be dead or they could simply be missing or they are living somewhere you can't trace them?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not only that. The elections are voluntary. Some people didn't register to vote. We only have information about those who registered to vote. So that is still this little group, little group. We think this group is little because ICRC expresses the view that the participation in the elections, municipal elections 1997, was rather high. They say 75 per cent. In some reports they even mention up to 88 per cent of the eligible voters registered to vote. So our sample is large but doesn't include everyone who survived these difficult years of the war and we don't have -- we don't included all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The difference, I think is about 4.600, but we can't place any significance on that figure. It's simply you cannot trace them for one reason or another.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is some sort of a minimum number. You can see it this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, I think children are not included?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because they're only registered to vote as of 18. So everybody between 0 and 17 wouldn't be reflected in those numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: But if I may add, the population shown in table 3B is the same age. So we control for age. We were here. We formed the same control of those who were eligible to vote in 1997 elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not so much eligible but who registered to vote.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not so much eligible to vote but who registered to vote.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Who registered to vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And both of these tables, figure 3A and figure 3B, each of them are based upon that one controlled figure, those who are registered to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, to summarise, does it mean it is actually a conservative approach you adopted because you only had a sample number and not the absolute numbers of survivors?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I would put it this way: The sample we show here is a big-sized sample and must be seen as reliable. So the conclusions that we draw on the basis of this sample, in terms of relative measures like percentages, are reliable, in my view. But if we are interested in showing absolute size of certain groups in the population, how large was the size of Muslim population in 1997, or Serb or any other ethnic population, then I must say our numbers are minimum numbers. So these are the numbers that we are hundred per cent sure these people were alive in 1997 and registered to vote. But -- and this I can agree that this means our approach is conservative. We don't show more than we absolutely hundred per cent are sure were alive in this period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we please go to the next map of the Muslim displacement.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Perhaps may I conclude on this presentation? Because actually, so far I haven't been able to say what is the main conclusion shown in figure 1B and table 3B. In table 3B, in the first column, those who were identified for 1997 in this municipality means in the Visegrad municipality, are, as you see, Serbs. Serbs. This is quite a large group that stayed in this municipality and didn't move to other municipalities. In relative terms, 96 -- almost 97 per cent of Serbs who used to live in Visegrad in 1991, stayed, still lived in this municipality in 1997. If you then compare the first column, this first municipality with the next one, other municipality, then you see the number of people who moved from Visegrad to other municipalities within Bosnia and Herzegovina, these other displaced persons, and in this column, the largest group are Muslims. Other groups are minor among those displaced persons. And the next column shows those who left the country and moved from Visegrad just abroad. And again the same situation. The largest group among those who migrated are the Muslims. So what I'm trying to say is that it is rather obvious that Muslims are the group who actually was not found in figure 1 and table 1 -- 3A in this municipality in 1997, because, as we see, they just left the municipality and moved elsewhere, either to other municipalities or to other countries. This is the conclusion shown here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the map 1C that you prepared outline where the Muslims left to predominantly?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got a different version, Ms. Bauer? My doesn't have 1C on it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. This is my probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I've got the document.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: -- mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It is in the report referred to as 1C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This map illustrates the displacements of the Muslims from the Visegrad municipality, and what is also marked on the map with red colour is the Dayton line, which shows the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska. Visegrad, of course, is located in Republika Srpska. The municipalities which are marked on the map with green colour, starting from light green up to dark, very dark green, are all municipalities where the Muslims went to. The darker the colour, the larger the group of Muslims moved into a particular municipality. It is clear that large groups of Muslims moved to Gorazde, then to several municipalities located in Sarajevo. It is -- Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo. It is Hadzici, Vogosca, Ilijas, Ilidza, and not marked on the map, but because of the very small size of these municipalities, which is a very difficult problem just to mark them, but in the report Centar, Stari Grad and Novo Sarajevo are mentioned as well. Also three municipalities in the surroundings of Sarajevo: Zenica, Kakanj, and Visoko, were the municipalities where the Muslim population moved to from the Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one can conclude that in 1997, all internally displaced Muslims lived in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. All these municipalities are located in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Should we go on to the next subject or rather go there after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's use up the three minutes. These adjournments get longer and longer if you start chipping them away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next table, table number 6. Did you establish a rank of selected municipalities in the Visegrad -- selected municipalities and compared the ethnic composition in Visegrad compared to the other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is what is this table about. It was actually very challenging to us to understand the scale of the change in the ethnic composition in Visegrad, and the only way to conclude, to assess the scale of changes was to compare Visegrad with other municipalities. This is why we selected, in addition to Visegrad, some more municipalities. All the municipalities selected are located in the close neighbourhood of Visegrad. In the report, we included just in the beginning a reference map of this region of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is very clear from this map that the municipalities on our list are in the direct neighbourhood of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this table show in conclusion that the most dramatic changes in the ethnic composition occurred in Visegrad after the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is the conclusion. If you look at the last column in this table, which is called chi-squared statistic. It is just the name of this statistic that was used as a tool, statistical tool to establish the ranking, the highest value of this statistic is shown for Srebrenica. Visegrad is the second place. Generally the higher the value of this statistic, the larger the change, the larger the disagreement of the two distributions, 1991 and 1997 distribution, ethnic distribution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does this table also show that there was a pattern in the region, a region which then entirely became Serb after the war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It is very clear if in addition to the statistic, you take a look at the columns, just ethnic composition shown for Serbs and Muslims. If you study carefully these figures, it is clear that the Muslims actually disappeared almost completely from all these municipalities in 1997 and the opposite is shown for Serbs. This is -- this can be called a pattern. This is what is the underlying reason for the value -- high values of the chi-squared statistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But each of those municipalities is now in Republika Srpska. I think that was the purpose of the question?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. I think the municipalities, all of them, are in Republika Srpska. So this is an analysis which shows the pattern that is identified for the Serb part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a small area of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think we'll take the adjournment now. We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, the last examination you did was the demographic distribution of missing persons, based on the ICRC missing persons list. Could we go, please, to figure 2. Could you explain, please, what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It needs a slight addition to it, which you can take from the report itself. Those on the left are males and those on the right are females.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understood what you said. It is related to the figure number 2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Figure number 2.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is a presentation which shows men to the left and women to the right, and in this figure, age groups are shown starting from 0 to 14 years, next one is 15 to 29, next one is 30, 44 years, and so on up to -- the last one is 75 plus, all ages above 75 years. And the scale here is just percentages, are percentages. If I'm correct. No, I'm sorry. These are just numbers. These are just numbers. I'm sorry. These are absolute numbers. So the size of each group, age group, which was listed in the ICRC list of missing persons separately here on the left for men and for women to the right. The conclusion related to the analysis shown in figure 2 is that those who were missing most frequently were men at younger, military age, from, say, 15 to 44 years. In total, as it was mentioned before, we have analysed 570 [sic] missing persons. These are those whose names have been verified by linking with the census information. Out of these 517, 499 were Muslims, and 18 persons were of other ethnicity. I should perhaps mention here that in the context of ethnicity, of the analysis made by ethnicity, that ICRC list of missing persons doesn't include information about ethnicity, but because we linked those records from the ICRC missing persons list with the census, we obtained the information about ethnicity from that census files. This is actually very important that the same definition of ethnicity is used in these type of comparisons, because people tend to change their own views about whether they are Muslims or Croats or any other group. It is guaranteed in our report that all information about ethnicity is consistent, because the same definition as reported in that census was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, you once said 570 and then 517, but it was 17?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Seventeen, 17, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, because it said 70 at one point. Did you also look into what time period most disappearances occurred in the Visegrad municipality?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It was possible, because information about the date of disappearance is included in the ICRC information -- list. It is the date the person was last seen. It is very specific information, which includes almost always day and month. It is not necessarily the date of death, although generally it is assumed that the persons listed as missing are dead. In the figure number 4 below, we show the period from 1st of April until end of June, 30th of June, and for each day in this period, we show the number of persons who went missing on a particular day. It is clear -- well, I should have started from a general conclusion that actually these two months, April and June, are the months where most people disappeared, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mean May and June.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, May and June, yes. These are three months. I'm sorry. I'm thinking about perhaps too many details right now. May and June are the two months where most people indeed disappeared. And in this period, May and June, three days with the highest number of people who went missing on these days are in June. It is 14th of June and 20th of June; and in May, it is the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is also remarkable, all these bars also show, by using different colours, the ethnic composition of those who went missing. The green colour is consequently used for the Muslims. So it is clear that also in the analysis of timing, the conclusion of Muslims most frequently going missing is confirmed. In the final analysis -- this is next page, please, table 11 -- was made in order to compare the situation in Visegrad, Visegrad municipality, with a number of selected municipalities. The list of selected is exactly the same as the list used in the ranking of municipalities due to the scale of changes in ethnic composition. The period is since -- from April 1992 until December 1992, and it is again confirmed here that May and June 1992 were the two months with most disappearances. And Visegrad is actually the municipality which observed the largest, the highest numbers of persons who went missing in this period. It is altogether in May and June 1992 that, in total, 62 per cent, approximately 62 per cent of persons in this area went missing. So it is typical what we have found for Visegrad, for the whole area that has been analysed in our study.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this table, to conclude, does it also refer that during that time period, a larger scale process of disappearing people was taking place in the whole area?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I definitely agree that this can be seen as a large-scale process in this period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is now the area of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, which is now an area in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet. Cross-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I'm interested in this list of missing persons, and you explained that the dates on the list and the locations indicate the last date or place where that person was seen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Excuse me. I -- could the interpreter repeat the question, please? I didn't have my headphones on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the list of missing persons, you explained, madam, that the dates on the list and the places indicated are the last date and place that person was seen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is the date that the persons who were reported missing were last seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to me what it means when on the date next to the month there are two zeros. Does that mean that the exact date is not known or does it mean the beginning or the end of the month when that person went missing?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The two zeros are always used when the day or month is unknown. So it is not the beginning or the end, it is an unknown date or month of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Though it is stated in your report that this is a list of missing persons, I am referring to point 2.3 on page 6, that this is primarily a list of missing persons and not of persons deceased, though it is assumed that most of them, if not all of them, are no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The list of missing persons, this is correct, but ICRC themselves expressed the opinion that the persons are most likely dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, to what extent is this list accurate? Is there a possibility for there to be fewer or larger numbers of people missing that do not appear on this list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is indeed a list that cannot be seen as complete, but -- well, first of all, it is the most complete source of information about missing persons that exists. There is no other more complete source different than ICRC list of missing persons. In order to assess to what extent it is complete as such, we would need some information about the actual number of missing persons that is unknown. I believe strongly that this is a relatively complete source, but I am unable to say what is the coverage of the source, for the percentage terms, quantitatively. I'm unable to assess this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, there is a witness being called who I think will probably be able to give you more explanation about the ICRC list. I've forgotten his name, but he's the head of the missing persons organisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, yes. He gave evidence in the Krnojelac case, and I assure you he can go on for hours about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will not dwell on this list any further as I have received sufficient information from the answers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: If I may add one thing. I think that the list should be as a reliable source of information in comparative studies of the type as we presented for Visegrad and surrounding municipalities. There is no reason to believe that for some areas the list was more complete than for other areas. The approach ICRC used when collecting this information was exactly the same in all municipalities. So the pattern seen in comparisons of different municipalities I would think is reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I understood, in this particular case, you gave us the situation in Visegrad, but you also took into account certain other municipalities in the surroundings. Did you cover other municipalities in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? In other words, could you tell me whether you had data for municipalities which after Dayton became part of the Federation and in which the Serb population had been in the majority and no longer is, that is, no longer in 1997? Did you investigate those cases, perhaps in other cases in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, not in this report, but we do process information about other municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course, information about ethnic composition and changes in the ethnic composition, and indeed, there were municipalities in the Federation where the opposite type of population changes was seen. This is what I can say, but I am unable to present these results right now because these are results which are not part of this particular report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
