utterances.text: When you were examining the percentage share of the Serb population in Visegrad in 1997, did this apply to the same population that was there in 1991 or did it include the Serbs who lived in Visegrad municipality in 1997 but had not lived there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We actually presented two different types of analyses. The first analysis I discussed today based on figure 1A and table 3A was made by -- in terms of de facto population. This means two populations in 1991, 1997, two de facto populations were compared in this analysis. This would mean that also for 1997, also Serbs, newcomers in Visegrad were included, because de facto means we took information about those who de facto were there, lived there in these two periods, in these two analysed periods. But in the next analysis that is shown in our report in figure 1B and table 3B, we took a different perspective. We only analysed those who originally lived in 1991, and we concentrated on showing their location in 1997. So this means the original Serb population, the original Muslim population, Croat, and others population. So we actually did both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you this, among other things, because you explained that for the year 1997, as one of the main sources, you used the voters' registry.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in Visegrad, at this point in time, there are more inhabitants than there used to be before the war because several thousand people came as refugees from Herzegovina, mostly from Konjic, but as far as I know, they are still registered in voters' registers as voters in Herzegovina or Konjic. So were these persons also as inhabitants of Visegrad or because they are voters' registers outside Visegrad they were not included?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The information that we used to define the place of residence in 1997 is the municipality of registration. Municipality of registration is one of the items included in the voters' register that inform about the residence of the voters in 1997. Next to this item we could have used, for instance, the self-reported municipality of residence in 1997, but we believe that the self-reported information is less reliable than the information which is just actual registration. We believe that the voters registered to vote, where they actually lived or stayed at the moment of registration. So I don't think that the voters from other municipalities in Bosnia who actually stayed in the municipality of Visegrad were registered in the old municipalities. There was no need to do so. Even if someone wanted to vote for the municipality where the person lived in 1991, it was possible to do in the municipality where the person registered to vote, where the person actually stayed in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is the result of that answer this: That there may have been other people of Serb ethnicity living in the Visegrad municipality in 1997 who were still registered in some municipalities of the Federation but who had come to Visegrad as refugees without registering there? That, as I understood it, was the purpose of the question.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, -- well, as far as I understand it, the municipality of registration is the best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, please.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We understand why you have selected it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But what I understood Mr. Domazet to be suggesting is that there could be other people of Serb ethnicity who were still registered somewhere in the Federation but who had come to the Visegrad municipality as refugees and they would not be included in your figures. It seems to follow to me the answer to that is that is correct, but that was the purpose of the question.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah. Perhaps. This is my answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what you were after, wasn't it, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood your answers correctly, the actual voters' register is not the most reliable source, as it is possible for someone not to have registered. But my question is: Did you check whether there may be people on the voters' register who may also be on the missing persons list and in that way to verify the accuracy of this list? That is, do you know whether perhaps the International Red Cross did that, if that was not part of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is always part of our analysis to compare the different lists and to exclude cases that are obviously contradictory, and this is what we have done in this case. Perhaps there were a few cases, like two or something like that, but this wasn't an issue at all in this particular case. So what we present are lists that are, first of all, gleaned from duplicates. This is one thing. Every list, ICRC, voters, there are no duplicates. We have means to check for duplicates. This is one thing. And secondly, we can cross-compare the list, cross-examine the lists in order not to show that someone reported as missing as a voter, a registered voter. And all the lists are verified by linking with the population census 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you, please, to look at figure 4, the number of persons missing in Visegrad in the period April/June 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that according to this figure, on the 14 the of June, most persons went missing, according to this figure. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, 14th of June was one of the three days I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. How many persons would it be, judging by this diagram? I would say it would be 26, but could you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is approximately 26. If you need specific number, I would have to check whether it was 26 or 27, but in my view, it is 26 too. I don't have the figures that were used for this diagram right now in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, the line marked 25 stands for the number of missing persons, that is, these numbers indicated on the left, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Excuse me, once again, please, if you may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the left-hand side of the diagram, figure number 4, the numbers 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25, to my understanding, stand for the number of missing persons so that on the 14th of June, about 26 went missing. It may be plus, minus one, but roughly that figure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Just one question. Re-examined by Ms. Bauer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, the 26 people that went missing that day are 26 people that were reported in the ICRC list as missing. It don't necessarily mean that only 26 people went missing that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And moreover, these are people whose identity is verified. No. Excuse me. The ethnicity is included. So this is the number listed in the ICRC list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And perhaps more specifically, it was 26 people who were reported to the ICRC as having last been seen on the 26th of June?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. There have been -- there might have been more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the reports were coming from from the ICRC? Who would usually report those?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Usually these were family members, close relatives. In some exceptional cases neighbours who were eyewitnesses. ICRC didn't accept reports from people whose relation to the missing person was unclear, unknown, not well defined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just correct the record. We are talking about the 14th of June, not the 26th of June. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both dates have the same figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, may I just ask you a couple of questions about page 1 of your report. I'm curious to know what you identify as Yugoslav ethnicity in the first of your major findings. Is that people from the former Yugoslavia or from Serbia and Montenegro or what?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These Yugoslavs is just how people reported themselves in that census. It was an open-ended question, and everybody was free to decide, to say, to mention what ethnicity he or she was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So they could be Serbs or Croats?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We just don't know.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: But this is how they identified themselves, not as Serbs, or Croats, or Muslims, Yugoslavs,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand. Now, in your third finding, you referred just to Visegrad. Should we assume that is a reference to the municipality and not the town?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, thank you very much for coming along to give evidence, and we thank you for your evidence, and you are free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer, do you want to tender that document which is marked 41.2? It's not yet in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection to that, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is extracts from the other report

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Exactly. I think it is more detailed in one case and in another case a little bit more simplified in the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that will be Exhibit P41.2. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls its next witness, VG61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there a pseudonym document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P79, and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you please make the solemn declaration in the document which is being shown to you by the court usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P79 Examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 61, I'd ask you to look at the name, the date of birth, and the address at the top of that document. Do you recognise that information as that to be of yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would just remind you, in the course of your testimony, if you need to refer to some other witnesses, we have assigned some of the witnesses numbers and they are also indicated on that document P79. Witness 61, I would ask you to briefly describe your background for the Chamber. I'm most concerned with your professional background.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Well, I am a former policeman by profession. I am retired. I have ended my years of service. I have lived in the town of Visegrad, Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am the father of two children. I was married. My wife died. I'm a widower, and now I live in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and more specifically in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you a police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Well, I was a policeman in Visegrad until the aggression of 1992. I lived in Visegrad until May 31, 1993, until our territory succumbed, the territory in Visegrad, and then I moved to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, when did you leave Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Well, I left Visegrad -- I'm not quite sure. I don't know whether it was April 5th or 6th. That was the last time I was in my house in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was April 5th or 6th of 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many years were you a police officer in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: In Visegrad, I worked as a police officer [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of your employment at the Visegrad police station, did you have occasion to investigate crimes and interview witnesses of crimes or victims of crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the day that you left Visegrad. Can you tell us why you left Visegrad on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: I left Visegrad that day because the police station that existed in Medjedja, I was the commander of the station and I was on duty there, and that's why I left the city. I was not safe because I was threatened by telephone and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you be specific about what types of threats you received?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: On two occasions by telephone, they told me if I continued to do my business there, I would be liquidated, me and my family and everyone. But I didn't leave the place because I was scared. I did it because of my duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said -- when this person threatened you and said "continue your business," did you understand that to mean your responsibilities as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you leave Visegrad alone or did you take your entire family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: I left alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you left Visegrad, was it possible for you to communicate with people in Visegrad by way of the telephone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us an idea about how many times per week would you speak with friends or family from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Well, perhaps in a few days -- well, once a week or a few times a week or not at all, because the connections were bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the members of your family that remained behind in Visegrad, was your father one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: No. He was in the village where I was born, six kilometres from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he remain in that village at the time that you had left Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you learnt about a fire that took place in the area of Pionirska Street? And I would just remind you in your answer, if you need to refer to a witness, please look at the sheet P79 before you. Did you ever learn of a fire in Visegrad on Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed about the fire in Pionirska Street in Visegrad by Witness 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you when Witness 13 informed you about the fire in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Well, at the time, I was at my workplace when Witness 13 came. He was wounded on his right arm, and the witness told me how the whole event took place. The people, the residents that had been expelled from the village where they were living, and they were taken by foot to the town. Well, I cannot quote exact figures. There were about between 50 and 60 persons, elderly people, sick people, children, and other citizens joined them along the way. Not really joined them but were forced to join them, people who were at the time in Sase. They had to join these people, and they were taken to Visegrad, to the Red Cross there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 61, you said you were at your workplace when Witness VG13 spoke to you about this. Was your workplace a police station in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Witness VG13 inform you that your father was among one of the people -- one of the victims of that fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Witness 13 told me about the whole event, and in the meantime, he told me that this had happened to my -- to my family but that they had left to the place called Olovo, near Kladanj. And two or three days later, Witness 13 told me that my father had been there, my mother, two sisters, and a boy of 12 years old. He was the son of one of my sisters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you spoke to your father regarding what happened that night in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: No. My first meeting with my father, my first contact, took place February 24, 1993, in a place called Donja Zimca, municipality of Visoko, where my father was placed in a collective centre in an elementary school, but I don't know the name of that school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequent to February 24th of 1993, did you have several conversations with your father regarding what happened on the night of the fire in Visegrad on Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Well, at least five or six times I talked to my father during his lifetime. He died in 1996. I can tell you the exact date when he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please do that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: My father died September 10th, 1996, in Sarajevo. He was buried in Sarajevo, at the municipal cemetery, and it is called Alfakovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to describe for the Chamber as best you're able to recount your father's description of what happened on -- during the fire on Pionirska Street. And let us begin by did he tell you the date on which this fire took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. It happened exactly between June 13 and 14. Well, to be accurate, between 2330 and 2400 hours. People were taken from one house in Pionirska where they had been until then on that critical day, when they were returned from the hotel, and they were told that they would travel only the next day to Olovo because there were no buses available. So on that critical night, the time I mentioned, 2330 hours and 2400 hours, from the house in Pionirska Street, where people had been expelled from that house to another house which is near a creek which is about 70 to 80 metres from the house where they had previously been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father -- excuse me. When you spoke with your father regarding this incident, would it be fair to say that you not only spoke to him as his son but also as a police officer investigating a crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. I was interested in every detail specifically. I was interested in how the whole thing evolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask your father who the people were who were involved in this fire, the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Well, on that critical day, specifically at the time when at about 2.00 p.m. people were brought to that house, Milan Lukic was there, Sredoje Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and in the immediate vicinity of that house, there was Bosko Djuric, Zoran Joksimovic, Susnjar is another person. That's his surname. His nickname is Lalco. I don't know his exact name. And at that critical point in time, there was also Ilic. His nickname was Mikan. I know him by the nickname of Mikan. He was a teacher at the elementary school in Prelovo, 12 kilometres away from Visegrad, north in the direction of the municipality of Rogatica. About 2.00, 2.00 p.m., they were in the immediate vicinity when Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic entered the house, issued an order that no one could move from the house. They said that anyone who had any money, foreign currency, jewellery, that they should put it on a table, in a bag which was on that table. If they didn't do so, they would be searched. And if they found anything on anyone of the objects mentioned, the person would be liquidated. After the money and jewellery had been collected, they took out a woman. Well, I would just like to look at the name. It is the wife of Dzevad Kurspahic. She is a nice looking young woman and another woman whom I did not know. I think her name was Jasmina but I don't know where she was from. She joined us on the way. She joined the column that was actually herded in the place of Sase. After that, the other people that I mentioned that were around the house, Milan Lukic informed us that no one could move out of the house until he returned. After that, all three of them moved away. My father had said that they went to a place called Bikavac, a motel in Visegrad, and about -- I don't know exactly the time. I think it was around 10.00 p.m., between 10.00 and 11.00, they reappeared at that house where they continued to harass us, to search, to see if any objects had been missed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that "they returned to the house." Did your father identify any of the men or the people who returned to the house later in the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. Mitar Vasiljevic, Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and another man who was mentioned. I subsequently learned that this person was from Ilijas, from the municipality of Ilijas, who is now living in Visegrad. He was the first associate of Milan Lukic. He is blonde, exceptionally blonde, with long blonde hair, and Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic wore a large hat on that critical day. Whether it was white or yellow, something like that. I don't believe my father could distinguish between colours very well to be very accurate. The four of them entered that house between 10.00 p.m. and 11.00 p.m. on that critical night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father describe the shape of the hat that Mitar Vasiljevic was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: He said it was a big round hat. His impression was that it was a big hat and that it was very peculiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father indicate where he knew this person he's identifying as Mitar Vasiljevic from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Well, I can say that Mitar Vasiljevic, for about 20 years, perhaps less or more, had been a waiter in Visegrad, and he worked in many restaurants of Panos. At least about 50 times at least he served these people in motels and hotels, and they knew him personally. And amongst them, he knew my father personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you to describe in great specificity what exactly your father told you Mitar Vasiljevic did at this time between 10.00 and 11.00 at night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really say. I know that some of them had said that they would be moved to another house because they had been attacking the Green Berets, because shots were heard at that critical point near the house where they were. And then there was -- people were evacuated from that house to another house where they were -- which was burnt down, and in front of that house, when they were going out and when they were escorted to another house, they were in a row and on one side, there was Mitar Vasiljevic and the blonde chap whose name I didn't know. There was Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and Zoran Joksimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father describe for you how he escaped from the fire that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what he told you regarding his escape from the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: So as they were entering the second house which was burnt later, my father, who was not in good health, was the last to enter, and this man Susnjar, nicknamed Lalco, led in by hand through the door, and the room was so full that he remained right next to the door. He was more or less pushed inside. And then this door of this room was closed by Susnjar so that the door pushed him inside. When the door was locked, a powerful explosion was heard, because on this building there were two windows, and one of those windows was protected with metal wiring which was tied because there was no -- there were no windowpanes on this building as it hadn't yet been moved into. And the other window was also protected so that there was no way of getting out. In the immediate vicinity of this one window, one of my sisters was standing, and the father suggested that she jump out to save herself and her child. After this powerful explosion occurred, my father was wounded in the forehead, his right lower arm and upper arm. And after this explosion, there was a terrible scream and panic. And from the explosion, the door that -- the door was opened, blown open, so he was thrown outside on his back. Seeing that he hadn't been wounded in his legs and that he could get up, he rolled down a slope which is about 10 or 12 metres high, and below that there's a swamp, a creek that the sewage flows through which hasn't been repaired. And after that, ten minutes or so later, he moved to a bush of dry maize stems that had been in the form of a mound and hid there. And screams and cries could be heard from the house. He told me that this baby had a real baby's voice that you could hear was dying off slowly. And he stayed there in this mound all day while these guy were is waiting outside, and whoever jumped out of the building, they opened fire on them and killed them. At the end of that day, he left this place and went to a nearby locality on the outskirts of town towards Titovo Uzice. He was wearing woollen socks and no shoes, and he was wounded and bloody. After that he, stayed there two or three days, and after that, they came looking for him. They had probably heard that he had survived. I don't know. Among other things, he went by convoy from Visegrad, five or six days later. He had to put on women's clothing. He got onto a truck together with other locals from Visegrad, and they were transported to Olovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your father was led by the hand or by the arm into the building that was eventually set on fire. Was that because your father has trouble walking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Most probably that was the reason, or it was so full that he had to be pushed inside, shoved inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that your father described some of the things that he saw as he was hiding in this mound down by the creek. Did he Describe for you who the people were that were firing at the victims as they tried to escape? Did he identify those people to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: In view of the fact that it was night-time and they couldn't see, the people mentioned was Mitar, this fair-haired one whose name I don't know and nor does my father, the two Lukics, Milan and Sredoje, and this young man Zoran Joksimovic. At the critical time, they were the ones that escorted them there, put them in the building and they were probably the people who were around the building, but he couldn't see them because it was night-time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned a number of people as being involved as perpetrators in this act and you've described one as a blonde person whom you do not know. My question to you is: These other names that you have mentioned, are these all people that you know from your time living and working in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. I know all these men personally, with the exception of this blonde man whom I have never seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you certain that your father told you that Mitar Vasiljevic was present at the night when the house was actually set on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'd like to show a brief portion of a video, about 10 seconds, just to identify it, but it does include a depiction of this witness's father, so I'd ask that we go into private session for just a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're now in public session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 66, did there come a time when your father gave a videotaped account of what happened to him that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when approximately he gave that account?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: I know approximately. I don't know the exact date, but what could it have been? He stayed in Visegrad five or six days after the event, then three days in Olovo, from Olovo to Visoko it probably took him one day. So whether it was immediately after he arrived at Visoko or the next day, but in any event, it was probably the first day. So maybe ten days after the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So approximately ten days after the event, your father gave a videotaped account of what occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Ten to 12 days. It couldn't have been -- it shouldn't have been longer. Between 10 and 12 days, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: I saw this first recording in 1995, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the short portion that we played here in court in private session, is that a portion of the video that you're now describing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it for the first time in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the video that you -- the entire -- have you observed or looked at this entire video from start to finish?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever he said, the statement he made for television, I saw it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it fairly and accurately depict your father describing what happened on the 14th -- 13th or 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The formula you use I frankly do not understand, and I do not understand how this witness could accede to that. Was he there when it was videoed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then how can he say something fairly and accurately represents something?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'm basing that on he knows his father's voice, he knows his father's appearance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then he could be asked whether that's his father's voice. It could be mutilated by cutting out words out here, there, and everywhere. It's obviously some constitutional case in the United States that says it has to fairly and accurately represent something, but it doesn't really mean anything, with all due respect, in this situation. If this video gets into evidence, it will be subject to any question about could it have been interfered with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness of 66, during the entire course of the video that you have watched, is it your father who is on that video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the voice that purports to be your father's voice, do you recognise it as your father's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes, accurately. I have this recording in my own possession. If necessary, I can show it and I can produce it. I think it is identical, absolutely 1 million per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would tender Prosecution video number 145 into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, but I would like this exhibit to be tendered after the examination of the witness, the completion of the witness's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That seems to be fair enough. If there's going to be a challenge to it, you'll have will the opportunity to re-examine, Mr. Groome, so I think we better reserve that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'll reserve my tendering of the transcripts of that until that time as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to look at Prosecution document number 147. Looking at document Prosecution number 147, is this a list of names that I asked you to review earlier this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you are related in some manner to each of the people listed on this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. All these surnames are relatives of mine, people with the same surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that since 1992, the time of this fire, you have not seen or heard from any of the people listed on this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: I have not seen any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender into evidence Prosecution number 147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Wouldn't you have to show that they were alive at least on the day of the fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can do that with another witness, Your Honour. I'm just introducing it at this stage to indicate that this witness has not seen these people since the day of the fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's the heading which concerns me, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would agree to strike that if the Court so wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree, Your Honour, if this could be of assistance for one of the witnesses to testify about these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, does that mean that you don't object to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what it means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Groome, there are some very minor differences. For example, number 19 does not have an "S" as a fourth letter like most of the others. I don't know whether that's deliberate. But what I'm more concerned about was the generality of the question and answer. The witness had earlier said all those with the same surname were relatives of his. There is one, number 36, who is described as a relative, even though she does not have the same surname, but then you have 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, and 51 which do not appear, on the face of them, to have the same surname, nor do they appear to have any relationship to him. Now, it was a very general question you asked and is the very general answer intended to refer to those?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll clear that up for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you should.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 61, as the Court has just indicated, you have identified the commonness of your surname with many of the people on this list. The other people who have different surnames, have you had an opportunity to review those names as well? And my first question will be: Are they people that you are either related to or that know personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have stated that the persons with the surname [redacted] are my relatives. I think I made myself clear. Those with the surname [redacted] are my relatives. As for [redacted] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. Please don't use the names. We are going to have to take those out of the transcript because they will identify you. Just refer to any in the list by the number beside them so that we don't broadcast your name to everybody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Thank you. So I was saying up to 43, they were all closely related, friends, neighbours, because I lived in this village. Number 44 is my sister. Number 45 is my sister's son. Number 46 and 47 are friends, that is, the in-laws of my nephew. The other numbers are all my acquaintances whom I would see frequently and have contact with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you had contact with any of the people on this list since 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just amend my tendering of this exhibit to tender it under seal given the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, most certainly, but at this stage the heading on it is not part of exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will replace it after lunch, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, we'll just put a line through it. That will be Exhibit P147 and it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived in Holland to testify here today last night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you brought with you numerous photographs of the people on this list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Not a large number, but I have photographs of all members of my immediate family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are willing to make them available to the Tribunal in this -- in the trial of this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Only if they could be photocopied in your presence. I would like to have the originals back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet. Cross-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said at the beginning, in answering questions from Mr. Groome, that you learnt about the fire in Pionirska Street from Witness VG13; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me when that was and in what way did she tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: I can. I can't remember the exact date. It was roughly about ten days after the event in Medjedja near Visegrad. My contact occurred with this witness occurred then, and she described to me the actual event, but he said that my family were not among them, that they had left for Olovo. And then two days later, probably to spare my feelings, he told me what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this witness came to you in Medjedja about ten days after the event and told you the story without telling you immediately that your close family members had died, nor did he mention that they were in that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: This witness told me that my family had gone to Olovo. Then two days later, he told me the whole story again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after this witness had told you the way it happened, a couple of days later, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Not after several days but after two days exactly. He told me that the whole village, all men, women, and children, all the villagers of the village had been brought to Visegrad and that they were taken to Pionirska Street to Memic Jusuf's house, from where, at the critical moment that I mentioned when it was, were transferred to a house which is 70 or 80 metres away, owned by Adem Omeragic, and that on the critical night, they were all se on fire in that house. And that she jumped out on the lower end through a window with her son, who is a survivor. They are alive. This son is alive, and they escaped through the creek towards a locality called Glavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were telling us about the event a moment ago, especially about the perpetrators, the Serbs, you were recounting the story on the basis of what your father told you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this witness who spoke to you tell you anything about it or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. The witness told me exactly the same story as my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say it was the identical story, does that mean to say that this witness mentioned these same persons that you listed a moment ago? So let me repeat. Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, Susnjar Lalco, this fair man from Ilijas, Joksimovic, that they were the participants who participated in one way or another in this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Witness number 13 only failed to mention Zoran Joksimovic at the critical moment that day. Maybe he forgot it or failed to notice, I don't know. And Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic and this blonde man whose name I don't know and she doesn't know it either, and Mitar Vasiljevic were there and took away the bag with the money from the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, this witness spoke to you first, and she was the first to mention these names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't quite understand. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the names that you have mentioned, with the possible exception of Zoran Joksimovic, you heard for the first time from Witness VG13?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you claim that those same names were mentioned by your father when you saw him for the first time in 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in assuming that your father lived in the village of Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: He was a farmer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time and before that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes. He was a man in his 70s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he know or could he have known all these persons that you mentioned today? Could he have known them personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of this blonde one, because he knows personally Sredoje Lukic, who had lunch in my father's house with me a hundred times. Mitar Vasiljevic must have served him at least 50 times, at least, in Panos Hotel and other restaurants in Visegrad town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did your father go to Visegrad so often and go to restaurants and coffee shops when Mr. Vasiljevic was on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Mr. Defence counsel, my father lived in the area of Visegrad for 70 years, and he went to that town at least 500 times. And Mr. Vasiljevic worked in Panos a long time, where people stayed and went to have lunch, because that was the kind of restaurant it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that your father went to that restaurant to have lunch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes, often with me, in my company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he know Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: He personally doesn't know Milan Lukic, but by the way, his associates called him -- Mitar and Sredoje, when they spoke to him, they used the word "Milan."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did he tell you that there was a person that was addressed as Milan or did he say that it was Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: He told me that they called him Milan Lukic, that he didn't know him personally, but as for all the others, from the other citizens and witnesses, let me be specific -- just a moment, please. Just a moment, please. From a person who is not on the list here or, rather, the person -- just a moment, please. Let me check. Let me think. The person under number 23 new him personally, because they went to school together. And she said that it was Milan Lukic, because they were in school together, in primary school for four years, in a place called Prelovo, close to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did this person, number 23, say this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: To all those who were present. She said that when they were brought to this building, that it was Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father tell you that or Witness VG13?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: Yes, my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, what you said a moment ago, that they called him by his name and surname, that is, Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: They called him by his name, Milan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said by the name Milan Lukic, and that has entered in the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG61
utterances.text: That may and mistake. Please correct that if that is what it says. The word used is "Milan."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
